title: How to Check AI’s Work
subtitle: The Verification Rulebook
description: A durable, practical method for turning fluent AI output into claims you can actually check.
audience: A newcomer using AI for everyday work who needs a proportionate way to decide what can be used, qualified, escalated or stopped.
learningObjective: Split an AI output into material claims, match each claim to adequate evidence, inspect support, scope and freshness, then record a qualified decision.
prerequisite: None. Episode 3 is a recommended story-led introduction, not a gate.
published: Not published — candidate under independent review
nextReview: Before any release, then annually for the durable method and quarterly for any named provider example.
whatCanChange: Provider features, plans, policies, interfaces, laws, statistics, research corrections and external links. The core checking method is reviewed annually or when learner evidence shows confusion.

opening.eyebrow: The LIBRAiRY · Reference Shelf · candidate under review
opening.promise: You do not need to redo every word. You need to find the parts that could change a decision, then check those properly.
opening.scenario: An AI turns meeting notes into a polished client update: “The client approved the revised launch date, expects a 20% lift and wants paid social added to phase one.” The notes actually say the client will review the date on Friday, somebody guessed “maybe 20%,” and paid social was only a question.
opening.question: Which part deserves attention first?

options.label: The polished wording
options.feedback: The wording is draft material. Keep it if it helps, but it is not the decision-changing risk.

options.label: Every sentence equally
options.feedback: Checking everything equally wastes effort. Triage the statements that could change action, commitment or harm.

options.label: The approval, lift and scope claims
options.feedback: Exactly. Those statements can commit money, timing or client expectations, so they need inspectable evidence.

chapters.title: Sort the output
chapters.dek: Fluency is presentation. Your first job is to identify what kind of thing each line is and what could change a decision.

sections.heading: Four useful buckets
paragraphs: A draft is proposed wording, structure or creative material. A factual claim says something checkable about the world. An assumption or inference connects facts without being directly stated. A recommendation proposes action and may depend on both facts and values.
A sentence can contain more than one bucket. Split compound statements before you search so one true clause cannot lend credibility to a false neighbour.
list: Draft: “Here is a warmer opening for the email.”
Claim: “The contract renews on 1 September.”
Inference: “The delay probably means the client is unhappy.”
Recommendation: “Move the campaign to September.”

sections.heading: Turn the stakes dial
paragraphs: Ask what happens if the statement is wrong, how reversible the action is, how uncertain the evidence is and how quickly the answer can change. A playlist caption and a medication decision do not deserve the same checking plan.
Check decision-changing claims first: money, deadlines, permissions, safety, public promises, people’s rights or anything hard to undo.

interaction.prompt: Classify all eight lines before checking your reasoning.

items.text: Here is a warmer opening for the email.

items.feedback: A date in a contract is externally checkable.

items.text: The delay probably means the client is unhappy.
items.feedback: The sentence interprets the delay; the client’s state is not directly established.

items.text: The free plan includes five seats.
items.feedback: A current plan limit is a checkable provider claim.

items.text: Five seats makes it the best plan for us.
items.feedback: “Best” is a decision that depends on requirements and values.

items.text: The client approved the new launch date.
items.feedback: Approval is a material, checkable commitment.
This is an interpretation, not a source-established fact.

chapters.title: Know what the tool actually did
chapters.dek: Search, grounding, citations and provenance can help. None of them is the same thing as verification.

definitions.definition: Creates the answer. Smooth language is not evidence.
Finds material. Finding a page does not make it the right page.
Connects or constrains an answer to supplied or retrieved material. The material can still be weak, stale, out of scope or misread.
Points to a source. The source must exist, open and support the nearby claim.
Records an asset’s origin or change history. It can help authenticate a trail without proving that the depicted event or assertion is true.
Connects a specific claim to adequate evidence under the right scope, date and stakes, then makes a qualified decision.

sections.heading: The chain
paragraphs: A source may be retrieved, summarized by a model and represented by a citation. The human check still asks whether the cited source is the right source and whether its exact content supports the exact claim.

The same model asking itself “are you sure?” may expose inconsistency, but it is not independent evidence. Independence comes from the underlying authoritative record, a qualified owner or a genuinely separate evidence path.

interaction.prompt: Match five artifacts to what they establish.

items.text: A tool returns a list of pages relevant to the query.
items.feedback: Finding material is retrieval; relevance and quality still need inspection.

items.text: The answer is constrained to a supplied policy document.
items.feedback: The model is grounded in the document; the document and interpretation can still be wrong or out of scope.

items.text: A numbered link points to a report.
items.feedback: The link is a pointer, not a support verdict.

items.text: Content Credentials bind an origin and edit history to an image.
items.feedback: The trail can be tamper-evident without proving the depicted event.

items.text: The exact claim is mapped to adequate, current, in-scope evidence and given a qualified verdict.
items.feedback: That is the claim-to-evidence decision process.

chapters.title: Frame the claim before searching
chapters.dek: A vague question retrieves vague evidence. Make the statement small enough to test.

sections.heading: Write the claim you actually need
paragraphs: Name the product or person, plan or version, place or jurisdiction, date, conditions, denominator and intended decision. Preserve qualifiers such as “may,” “in this sample” and “for eligible accounts.”

“She doesn’t even go here” is a useful scope reminder: evidence about a different plan, country or version may be real and still not apply. The film reference is only a mnemonic; it does not test the evidence for you.
list: Vague: “It is 50% faster.”
Checkable: “In the named study, people completing which task, compared with what baseline, finished 50% faster under which conditions?”
Vague: “The plan is free.”
Checkable: “Is this feature included in the provider’s free plan for Canadian individual accounts on 25 July 2026?”

interaction.prompt: Choose the repair that makes each claim checkable.

items.text: The new AI tool cuts admin time by 40%.
choices: Name the tool/version, population, task, baseline, period, method and source.
Ask the AI to sound less confident.
items.feedback: The repair exposes the denominator, comparison and method.

choices: Name provider, feature, plan, account type, region and date.
Treat free as a permanent product property.
items.feedback: Plan, account, region and date determine applicability.

items.text: The client approved Friday and expects a 20% lift.
choices: Split approval/date from forecast; name the decision record and forecast evidence.
items.feedback: Compound claims need separate evidence and verdicts.

chapters.title: Choose and inspect evidence
chapters.dek: There is no universal source ladder. Match evidence to the claim, then inspect what it actually says.

rows: Current feature, price, plan or policy
Current official documentation, account UI or contract; record region, plan and access date
AI memory, search snippet or undated screenshot
Current legislation, regulator, court or official authority; qualified professional for consequential application
Generic blog or a non-jurisdictional answer
Original paper, dataset and method; correction/retraction status; suitable expert synthesis
Press release or percentage without method/denominator
Original transcript, recording, filing, document or direct statement
Quote graphic, repost or citation without accessible source
Approved record, contract or named decision owner
Original asset/context plus provenance where present
Metadata treated as a truth verdict

sections.heading: The seven source questions
list: Identity: who created or published it, and what authority or interest do they have?
Relevance: does it address this exact claim rather than a nearby topic?
Scope: correct person, product, plan, place, jurisdiction and conditions?
Date/version: current enough for this decision?
Support: does it actually entail the claim, numbers and qualifiers?
Method: how was the evidence produced; what is missing or uncertain?
Independence: does corroboration trace to a genuinely separate origin?

interaction.prompt: You need today’s seat limit for a paid software plan in Canada. Compare all three, choose the most diagnostic source, then explain why and what you would inspect.

options.label: A popular forum answer from last year.
A search snippet quoting a review site.
The provider’s current Canadian plan page or authenticated plan terms, opened and dated.

interaction.feedback: The current applicable provider terms are the best starting source because they match owner, plan, region and date. A strong reason still inspects conditions and does not assume “official” means complete or infallible.

rubricDimensions.claim: The exact Canadian paid-plan seat-limit claim is framed.
rubricDimensions.evidence: The current applicable provider terms and exact clause are selected.
rubricDimensions.limitation: Conditions, omissions and the limit of an official source are named.
rubricDimensions.action: The source will be opened, inspected and recorded with plan, region and date.

chapters.title: Run the Receipt Loop
chapters.dek: Frame → Split → Find → Inspect → Cross-check → Decide → Record.

sections.heading: A worked decision
paragraphs: Return to the client update. Frame and split three claims: approval of the date, expected 20% lift and paid-social scope. Find the meeting record and named decision owner. Inspect the exact lines. The notes support none of the three as written.

The useful draft survives, but the claims change: “The client will review the proposed launch date Friday. The team discussed a possible lift but has not agreed a forecast. Paid social is an open scope question.”
list: SUPPORTED: adequate evidence supports the framed claim.
CONTRADICTED: adequate evidence conflicts with it.
UNRESOLVED: evidence is missing, mixed or too weak.
NOT APPLICABLE: the evidence addresses a different scope, version or question.

sections.heading: Record the decision receipt
paragraphs: Keep the exact claim, source, location, access date, scope, verdict, uncertainty and next review trigger. That turns a private moment of checking into a correction path.
Do not force a true/false answer when the honest result is unresolved. Abstaining from invented certainty is a useful outcome.

interaction.prompt: Complete the decision receipt before revealing the model answer.

rows.claim: Paid social is in phase one.
rows.source: Meeting notes list paid social as an open question.

interaction.feedback: Approval and paid-social scope are contradicted as written; the lift is unresolved. Preserve the useful draft, revise the claims and record owner, source, date and uncertainty.

rubricDimensions.claim: Approval, forecast and paid-social scope are split into separate claims.
rubricDimensions.evidence: Each verdict is mapped to the exact meeting-note passage.
rubricDimensions.limitation: The missing forecast source and pending decisions are preserved as uncertainty.
rubricDimensions.action: The draft will be revised and the decision owner, source and date recorded.

chapters.title: Currentness, media and independent checks
chapters.dek: A real source can be stale. A real provenance trail can accompany a false claim. A second answer can repeat the first answer’s blind spot.

sections.heading: Stale but real
paragraphs: A page may accurately describe an old model, plan, price or law and still be unusable for today’s decision. Record publication or version date, access date, region and change trigger.
Current provider examples belong in dated, replaceable cards—not inside the durable definition of verification.

sections.heading: Trace the origin
paragraphs: Five articles may repeat one press release. Corroboration requires separate provenance or evidence, not merely separate URLs.
For images, audio and video, provenance can help establish who made or changed an asset. Investigate the event, context and claim separately.

interaction.prompt: Resolve both cases and explain the evidence gap.

cases.label: Freshness case
cases.text: Three sites repeat a price from one provider page archived two years ago. Is that price established for today?
cases.feedback: It is one stale evidence chain. Check current applicable terms.

cases.label: Provenance case
cases.text: Valid Content Credentials identify an image’s origin and edits. Do they establish that its captioned event happened in Vancouver today?
cases.feedback: The provenance trail does not verify the event, place, date or caption.

rubricDimensions.claim: Today’s price and today’s captioned event are treated as separate claims.
rubricDimensions.evidence: Current plan terms and independent event/context records are identified.
rubricDimensions.limitation: Stale repetition and provenance-without-event-proof are named.
rubricDimensions.action: Freshness/scope and event place/date/context will be checked separately.

chapters.title: Use, qualify, escalate or stop
chapters.dek: The goal is a better decision—not infinite research or performative certainty.

sections.heading: Proportionate checking
list: Low and reversible: label it draft; one quick source inspection may be enough.
Material but reversible: use a claim table, authoritative source, scope/date check and independent corroboration where uncertainty remains.
High-stakes or hard to reverse: use authoritative records and the qualified human owner or professional. Stop or escalate when evidence is inadequate.

sections.heading: Write the honest answer
paragraphs: State what is supported, what remains uncertain, the scope and date, and what evidence would change the conclusion. A disclaimer does not repair bad advice.

This Rulebook is not legal, medical, financial, HR or safety advice. In those domains, it can help you organize questions and sources, but it cannot replace the responsible professional or decision owner.

interaction.prompt: Choose the proportionate next action for all three stakes levels.
choices: STOP AND ESCALATE TO QUALIFIED HUMAN

items.label: Low/reversible
items.text: An AI suggests three playful headings for an internal brainstorm.
items.feedback: Creative draft use is reversible; do not invent factual support.

items.label: Material/reversible
items.text: An AI compares current software plans for a team purchase.
items.feedback: Check current applicable terms, requirements and uncertainty before buying.

items.label: High/hard to reverse
items.text: An AI says to stop prescribed medication because a forum reports side effects.
items.answer: STOP AND ESCALATE TO QUALIFIED HUMAN
items.feedback: Do not act on the answer; contact the prescriber or appropriate medical professional.

promptCard.title: The source-bound prompt
promptCard.intro: Use this to reduce risk and expose missing evidence. It is not a truth machine.
promptCard.text: Answer only from the source material I provide or sources you can link directly. For every material claim: quote the exact supporting words and give the page, section or timestamp; if the source does not state it, write “not stated.” Separate source fact from inference. Add columns for source, publication/version date, access date and scope. Mark unsupported statements [needs receipt]. Preserve uncertainty and abstain when evidence is inadequate.
promptCard.warning: Now open the source yourself. This prompt cannot certify the source, the quote or the conclusion.

transferChallenge.title: The unseen transfer challenge
transferChallenge.scenario: A board memo says: “Tool A is the cheapest option for us, and a new study proves teams finish analysis 50% faster.” The linked price is for a different region and plan. The memo links a news story that mentions 50% but does not identify the task, baseline, sample or original study.
tasks: Choose the most diagnostic evidence action.
Name the scope and freshness checks.
Give a qualified verdict and state what would change it.

rubricDimensions.claim: Price, speed and “cheapest/best” are split into separate material claims.
rubricDimensions.evidence: Current like-for-like plan terms and the original study/method are selected.
rubricDimensions.limitation: Plan/region mismatch and missing task, baseline, sample and method are named.
rubricDimensions.action: The learner states what to inspect, what remains unresolved and what would change each verdict.

rubric: Price claim: UNRESOLVED or NOT APPLICABLE until the current official price for the correct plan, region, currency and date is inspected.
Speed claim: UNRESOLVED until the original study, population, task, baseline, denominator, method and correction status are inspected.
Best/cheapest recommendation: UNRESOLVED until relevant cost and requirements are compared, not only headline price.
A passing answer names evidence that can materially resolve the decision and does not claim the prompt guarantees accuracy.
